## Principle

In this chapter we will explore the principle of feedback control by looking at a common and instructive example, the control of liquid level in a tank. The arrangement is a simple one to describe. Liquid flows into the tank, and liquid flows out of it, and the task of the control loop is to hold the level of liquid in the tank at a desired value, which is known as the set point, even though the flows entering and leaving the tank may change over time.

The loop is made up of a number of elements that work together. A measuring device observes the level and produces a signal that represents it. A controller compares that signal with the set point and works out how the outflow needs to be adjusted. A valve on the outlet line then makes the adjustment. If the level rises above the set point, the controller opens the valve further so that more liquid leaves the tank, and if the level falls, the controller closes the valve so that less liquid leaves. The action is therefore always in the direction that opposes the change in level, and it is this opposition that makes the control a feedback arrangement.

The controller considered in this chapter is a proportional controller, which means that the change it makes to the outflow is proportional to the departure of the level from the set point. In the example used throughout this chapter, the numbers are as follows. The inflow to the tank is normally 10 cubic metres per hour, and at the set point the outflow matches it, so the level is steady. The controller is arranged so that the outflow changes by 5 cubic metres per hour for every metre by which the level departs from the set point. Suppose now that the inflow undergoes a step change, rising by 2 cubic metres per hour so that the inflow goes from 10 cubic metres per hour to a new value of 12 cubic metres per hour, and stays there.

An important consequence follows from the proportional action, and it is one that students often find surprising. The outflow can only change if the level changes, because it is the departure of the level from the set point that drives the controller. A sustained increase in the inflow therefore cannot be balanced at the original level. The level has to move to a new position, and to stay there, so that the valve is held open by exactly the extra amount that the new inflow requires. The permanent departure of the level from the set point that results is known as offset, and it is an inherent feature of proportional control rather than a defect of any particular controller.

## Equipment

The equipment of the loop consists of three main elements, together with the tank itself. The first element is the level transmitter, which is the sensor of the loop. Its job is to measure the level in the tank and to turn that measurement into a signal that can be transmitted to the controller. Different designs of transmitter sense the level in different ways, for example by the pressure at the base of the tank or by a float that rides on the surface of the liquid, but in every case the output of the device is a signal that stands for the level.

The second element is the controller itself. The controller receives the signal from the transmitter, compares it with the set point that the operator has chosen, and calculates the adjustment that is needed. In a modern plant the controller is usually an electronic or digital device, and the comparison and calculation happen inside it continuously.

The third element is the control valve on the outlet line, which is the final element of the loop. The valve is operated by an actuator that responds to the signal from the controller, opening or closing the valve so that the outflow changes. The valve is the only part of the loop that touches the process directly. It is also, in many ways, the least ideal part of the arrangement, because real valves have friction, they respond with a small delay, and the relationship between the signal they receive and the flow they pass is not perfectly regular. These imperfections matter for the limits discussed later in the chapter, but they do not change the principle.

## Worked example

We can now work through the example that was set up in the principle section, and the numbers used are exactly the numbers that were given there, with no new data introduced. The inflow steps up from 10 cubic metres per hour to 12 cubic metres per hour, which is an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour, and the question is to find where the level finally settles.

Immediately after the step, the outflow is still at its old value, because the level has not yet moved and the controller has had nothing to respond to. More liquid is therefore entering the tank than is leaving it, and the level begins to rise. As the level rises above the set point, the controller responds by opening the outlet valve, and the outflow increases. The level continues to rise, and the outflow continues to increase, until the two come back into balance.

The level settles when the outflow has increased by the same amount as the inflow, that is, by 2 cubic metres per hour. Since the outflow changes by 5 cubic metres per hour for every metre of departure from the set point, the departure that produces the required increase is given by 2 / 5 = 0.4 m. The level therefore settles at a new steady position that is above the set point, and the size of the offset in this example is 0.4 m.

The result can be checked by working backwards. At a departure of that size, the outflow has increased by exactly the amount of the inflow step, so inflow and outflow are once again equal, and there is no reason for the level to move any further. The offset is not a temporary feature of the adjustment; it is the permanent price that proportional control charges for balancing a sustained change in load, and it would only disappear if the controller were given an additional action that the simple proportional law does not contain.

## Limits

The account given in this chapter rests on a deliberately simple model, and it is important to be clear about the places where the simple model stops being an adequate description of a real loop. The first limitation is the offset itself, which has already been discussed. Proportional control balances a sustained change in inflow only by accepting a permanent departure from the set point, and for services in which the level has to be held close to its set point, that behaviour is not acceptable. Controllers used in practice therefore contain a further action that removes the offset over time, and that action brings its own complications, which the simple model does not describe at all.

A second limitation concerns the valve. The model treats the valve as though the outflow it passes were an exact and immediate function of the controller signal. Real valves depart from this in several ways: the flow they pass depends on the pressure drop across them as well as on their opening, the actuator takes time to move, and friction in the mechanism means that the valve does not always respond to a small change in signal. Each of these effects makes the real loop slower and less exact than the model suggests, and none of them is represented in the calculation of the worked example.

A third limitation is that the model says nothing about measurement. The transmitter is treated as though it reported the level instantly and exactly. Real measurements carry noise, and they lag behind the quantity being measured. A controller that responds to noise wastes valve movement, and a measurement lag can make a loop oscillate that the simple model predicts to be settled. Closely related to this is the question of disturbance size. A much larger disturbance than the modest step of the worked example can drive the valve to the end of its travel, at which point the controller loses its grip on the level altogether, and the proportional law no longer describes what happens.

Finally, the tank itself has been treated in the simplest possible way, as a vessel whose outflow is set entirely by the valve. In many real installations the outflow also depends on the level, because the level provides the head that drives the flow, and a tank of that kind is partly self-regulating: a rise in level increases the outflow even if the valve does not move. That behaviour changes the size of the offset and the speed of the response. The model of this chapter is therefore a starting point. It gives the structure of feedback, the meaning of offset, and the form of the calculation, and it holds for the ideal loop it describes; the loops of an operating plant require the further effects named here to be added to it.

## Principle

Feedback control holds a process variable at a set point by acting against the changes that disturb it. The example used throughout this chapter is the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid enters the tank and leaves it, and the level is the balance between the two flows at every instant. A level loop measures the level, compares it with the set point, and moves a valve on the outlet line so that the outflow opposes any change: level above the set point opens the valve further, and level below it closes the valve down. The action is called feedback because the measurement of the controlled variable is fed back into the action taken on it.

The controller in this chapter is proportional. A proportional controller changes the outflow in proportion to the error, the departure of the level from the set point, and it makes no other response. The data of the chapter are fixed here and are the only data the worked example uses. The inflow is normally 10 cubic metres per hour, matched at the set point by the outflow, so the level is steady. The controller changes the outflow by 5 cubic metres per hour for each metre of departure from the set point. The load change examined is a step in the inflow from 10 cubic metres per hour to a sustained 12 cubic metres per hour, an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour.

Offset follows from the proportional law, and it is the central result of the chapter. The outflow can change only when the level departs from the set point, because the departure is what the controller responds to. A sustained rise in inflow therefore cannot be balanced at the original level. The level moves to a new position and stays there, holding the valve open by the extra amount the new inflow requires. The permanent departure is called offset. Offset is inherent in proportional control; it is not a fault in a particular controller, and no adjustment of a purely proportional controller removes it while the law itself is kept.

## Equipment

The loop has three elements besides the tank: a transmitter, a controller, and a valve. Each element has one function, and the loop is the chain of the three.

The transmitter is the sensor. It measures the level and converts the measurement into a signal that can be sent to the controller. Transmitters sense level in different ways, by the pressure at the base of the tank, by a float on the surface, or by other means; the choice affects the measurement, and the limits section returns to it, but every design delivers the same thing to the loop, a signal that stands for the level.

The controller receives the signal, compares it with the set point, and computes the valve movement the error requires. The controller measures nothing and moves nothing. It is the decision element of the loop, and in a proportional loop its whole decision rule is the one proportion stated in the principle: outflow change against level departure.

The valve is the final element, the only part of the loop that acts on the process itself. An actuator drives it in response to the controller signal, and the outflow changes as it moves. The valve is also the least ideal element in the chain. Friction in its mechanism, the time its actuator takes to move, and the dependence of its flow on the pressure drop across it all separate the real valve from the valve of the principle, which passes exactly the flow its signal demands. The separation matters for practice; it does not change the structure of the loop.

## Worked example

The inflow steps from 10 cubic metres per hour to 12 cubic metres per hour, an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour, and the level's final position is required. The data are those of the principle section; no new data enter the calculation.

At the instant of the step the outflow is still at its former value, because the level has not moved and the controller has had no error to answer. Inflow exceeds outflow, and the level rises. The rise creates the error, the controller opens the valve against it, and the outflow grows as the level grows. Movement stops where the two flows are equal again.

Balance requires the outflow to grow by the amount of the step, 2 cubic metres per hour. The controller gives 5 cubic metres per hour of outflow change for each metre of departure, so the departure that yields the required change is 2 / 5 = 0.4 m. The level settles 0.4 m above the set point.

The check is the balance itself. At that departure the outflow has risen by exactly the inflow step, inflow and outflow are equal, and no further movement is driven. The offset is permanent under the proportional law: it is the position at which the loop can hold the new load, and it persists for as long as the load persists.

## Limits

The model of this chapter is an ideal loop, and its limits are the points where a real loop departs from the ideal. The limits are stated here in plain terms, because each of them is a place where a prediction from the model would mislead a reader who took it to the plant.

Offset is the first limit, and it is structural. Proportional control holds a new load only at a new level. Services that must hold level close to the set point need a controller with a further action that removes offset over time. That action exists in practice and is standard, but it is outside this model, and it brings behaviour, including the risk of oscillation, that the proportional calculation does not predict.

The valve is the second limit. The model gives the valve an exact, immediate response to its signal. A real valve passes a flow that depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening; its actuator takes time to travel; friction can hold it still against a small change of signal and then release it in a jump. The loop that results is slower and less exact than the model, and under a large disturbance the valve reaches the end of its travel. At full travel the controller has no action left, the proportional law has nothing to act through, and the level is uncontrolled until the disturbance retreats.

Measurement is the third limit. The model takes the transmitter signal as the level itself, delivered instantly and without error. A real measurement lags the level and carries noise. Lag adds delay to a loop whose stability depends on prompt action, and noise invites the controller to chase fluctuations that are not level changes at all, wearing the valve in the process.

The tank is the fourth limit. The model sets the outflow by the valve alone. In many installations the outflow also rises with the level, because the level supplies the head that drives flow through a fixed restriction, and such a tank is partly self-regulating: its level moves less for a given load change, and the offset is smaller than the chapter's calculation gives. The chapter's model is the limiting case in which none of that self-regulation exists.

The chapter's content is the structure of the feedback loop, the proportional law and the offset it forces, the three elements that carry the loop, and the calculation that turns a load step into a settling position. The limits named here mark where that content stops: at offset, at the real valve, at the real measurement, and at the real tank.
